## In the tutorial

Try each task in R before you open the answer. Tasks 1 to 4 use the Shark
Tank file, and money is measured in thousands of dollars (`ask_1k`). First
build the data for the analysis. The code is the same as in Lectures 4--6.

More practice for home is in the final section of this page,
[Extra practice for home](#i-ep02-home).

```{r}
#| label: iep02-load
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000
known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown")
known_gender$gender <- relevel(factor(known_gender$pitcher_gender_group),
                               ref = "all_men")
known_gender$ask_1k <- known_gender$ask_amount_usd / 1000
known_gender$women <- as.integer(
  known_gender$pitcher_gender_group %in% c("all_women", "mixed")
)
known_gender$season_c <- known_gender$season - mean(known_gender$season)
```

### Task 1: Multiple-regression coefficients (Lecture 4)

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} With all 1,441 pitches (`sharks`), fit a regression
of the equity offered, in percent (`equity_offered_pct`), on the season
(`season`), the requested amount in thousands of dollars (`ask_1k`), and the
number of words in the description (`description_words`).
Then answer these questions.

1. Interpret all three slopes with units and with the predictors that are
   held fixed, in one sentence each.
2. Say which 95% confidence interval of a slope includes zero, and report
   that interval.
3. Interpret $R^2$ and adjusted $R^2$ in one sentence each. Then name the
   two models that the overall F-test compares, and state its conclusion
   at the 5% level.
4. Give two reasons why the coefficients cannot be read as causal effects.

Use (copy and paste) this structure:

```text
R code:
Interpretation of the season slope:
Interpretation of the requested-amount slope:
Interpretation of the description-words slope:
Interval that includes zero:
R-squared:
Adjusted R-squared:
Overall F-test, the two models it compares, and its conclusion:
Two reasons why the coefficients are not causal effects:
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

```{r}
#| label: iep02-base-model
m1 <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + description_words,
  data = sharks
)
summary(m1)
confint(m1)
```

1. Among the 1,441 recorded pitches, at fixed values of the other included
   predictors:
   - one later season is associated with about 0.836 percentage points less
     equity offered, on average
   - an extra \$1,000 requested is associated with about 0.0029 percentage
     points less (about 0.29 points per \$100,000), on average
   - one additional description word is associated with about 0.128
     percentage points less, on average.
2. The interval for the description words, about $(-0.351, 0.095)$
   percentage points per word, includes zero.
3. $R^2\approx0.188$: the model explains about 19% of the variation in the
   equity offered among these pitches. Adjusted $R^2\approx0.186$ is almost
   the same, because the penalty for three predictors is small with 1,441
   pitches. The overall F-test compares the model with the intercept-only
   model. It gives $F\approx110.6$ on 3 and 1437 degrees of freedom, with a
   p-value below 0.001, so it rejects the null hypothesis that all three
   slopes are zero.
4. Any two of these: only selected pitches reach the show, the quality of
   the venture is not measured, the equity offered may influence the amount
   requested, and the variables may be measured with error.
:::

### Task 2: Dummy variables and a partial F-test (Lecture 5)

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Use the 1,434 pitches with a known team classification (`known_gender`).
Fit a reduced model of the equity offered (`equity_offered_pct`) on the
season and the requested amount (`ask_1k`). Fit a complete model that adds
the team category `gender` (all-men, all-women, or mixed).

1. Name the reference category.
2. Interpret both dummy coefficients, in one sentence each.
3. Test with a partial F-test at the 5% level, with the p-value approach,
   whether the two dummy coefficients are jointly zero.
4. Explain in one or two sentences why the partial F-test and the
   individual t-tests answer different questions.

Use (copy and paste) this structure:

```text
R code:
Reference category:
Interpretation of the all-women coefficient:
Interpretation of the mixed coefficient:
Null hypothesis H0:          and alternative hypothesis H1:
Test statistic formula:
Values in the formula:
Value of the test statistic:
P-value:
Conclusion:
Why the F-test and the t-tests answer different questions:
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

```{r}
#| label: iep02-gender-models
reduced <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k,
              data = known_gender)
complete <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + gender,
               data = known_gender)
summary(complete)
anova(reduced, complete)
```

1. The reference category is all-men.
2. At the same season and requested amount, all-women presenting teams are
   fitted to offer about 1.28 equity percentage points more than all-men
   teams, and mixed teams about 0.12 points more. The unit is percentage
   points, not percent. The categories are broad and the data do not come
   from an experiment, so the result does not show a causal effect of
   gender.
3. $H_0$: both dummy coefficients are zero. $H_1$: at least one of them is
   not zero. The test statistic is
   $F=\dfrac{(\text{SSE}_R-\text{SSE}_C)/q}{\text{SSE}_C/(n-k_C-1)}$, with
   $\text{SSE}_R=83{,}228$, $\text{SSE}_C=82{,}792$, $q=2$, and
   $n-k_C-1=1{,}429$. So
   $F=\dfrac{436.25/2}{82{,}792/1{,}429}\approx3.76$, with a p-value of
   about 0.023. Since $0.023\le0.05$, reject $H_0$ at the 5% level. The two
   terms are jointly significant.
4. The t-test of the mixed dummy alone (p $\approx$ 0.82) is far from
   significant, but the F-test rejects. The F-test asks whether the two
   terms together improve the model. Each t-test asks about one comparison
   with the reference category.
:::

### Task 3: Interaction (Lecture 6)

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} With the 1,434 pitches with a known team classification (`known_gender`),
fit a regression of the equity offered (`equity_offered_pct`) on the
centred season `season_c`, the dummy `women` (1 for all-women and mixed
teams), their interaction, and the requested amount (`ask_1k`).

1. Write the fitted line for `women = 0` and for `women = 1` at the
   average requested amount.
2. Calculate both season slopes.
3. Interpret the interaction estimate and its p-value in one or two
   sentences, without claiming too much in either direction.
4. Explain in one or two sentences what centring the season changes and
   what it does not change.

Use (copy and paste) this structure:

```text
R code:
Fitted line for women = 0:
Fitted line for women = 1:
Season slope for all-men teams:
Season slope for teams with women:
Interpretation of the interaction estimate and its p-value:
What centring changes and what it does not change:
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

```{r}
#| label: iep02-interaction
m_interaction <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k,
  data = known_gender
)
summary(m_interaction)
```

1. At the average requested amount, the fitted line for all-men teams is
   $12.866-0.799\,\text{season\_c}$, and for teams with women it is
   $13.673-0.861\,\text{season\_c}$, as in Lecture 6. The intercept 12.866
   is the intercept 13.625 plus the `ask_1k` coefficient times the average
   requested amount, `mean(known_gender$ask_1k)`. For teams with women the
   intercept is $12.866+0.807=13.673$.
2. The season slope is about $-0.799$ percentage points per season for
   all-men teams. For teams with women it is $-0.7994-0.0615\approx-0.861$.
3. The estimated difference in slopes is $-0.061$ percentage points per
   season, with p $\approx$ 0.520. The model gives no evidence that the
   season trends differ between the two groups. It also does not prove that
   the trends are equal, because the estimate is imprecise.
4. Centring makes the `women` coefficient compare the groups at the average
   season (about 8.8) and not at Season 0, which does not exist. It changes
   neither the fitted values nor the interaction estimate.
:::

### Task 4: Polynomial term (Lecture 6)

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} With all 1,441 pitches (`sharks`), fit a linear model of the equity
offered (`equity_offered_pct`) on the season and the requested amount
(`ask_1k`), and a quadratic model that adds the square of the season.

1. In an R formula, the square of `season` is written `I(season^2)`. Why
   is `I()` needed? Answer in one sentence.
2. Decide with a partial F-test at the 5% level whether the quadratic term
   improves the model.
3. Calculate the fitted change from Season 10 to Season 11, at the same
   requested amount.
4. State in one or two sentences why you should not extrapolate the curve
   beyond Season 16.

Use (copy and paste) this structure:

```text
R code:
Why I() is needed:
Null hypothesis H0:          and alternative hypothesis H1:
Value of the test statistic:
P-value:
Conclusion:
Fitted change from Season 10 to Season 11:
Why not to extrapolate beyond Season 16:
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

```{r}
#| label: iep02-polynomial
m_linear <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = sharks)
m_quadratic <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k,
  data = sharks
)
summary(m_quadratic)
anova(m_linear, m_quadratic)
```

1. `I()` tells R to calculate the square. Without `I()`, R would read `^`
   as part of the formula syntax and not as a square.
2. $H_0$: the coefficient of the quadratic term is zero. $H_1$: it is not
   zero. The partial F-test gives $F\approx20.1$ with p $<$ 0.001, so
   reject $H_0$ at the 5% level.
   The quadratic term improves the model.
3. With $\hat\beta_1\approx-1.713$ and $\hat\beta_2\approx0.051$, the
   change from Season 10 to 11 is
   $\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2(2\times10+1)=\hat\beta_1+21\hat\beta_2\approx-0.64$
   percentage points. Never read $\hat\beta_1$ alone while the quadratic
   term is in the model.
4. Beyond Season 16 the fitted curve turns upward, and no data support that
   turn. A quadratic curve can change direction sharply outside the observed
   range.
:::

### The models of Tasks 2 to 4 in one table {#iep02-spec-table}

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Lecture 4 showed how research papers put several models side by side in one
regression table. The table below does this for the models of Tasks 2 to 4.
All columns of such a table must use the same observations. Tasks 2 and 3
use the 1,434 pitches with a known team classification (`known_gender`).
Task 4 uses all 1,441 pitches. So first fit the quadratic model again on the
1,434 pitches. The code then prints the two model outputs that the answers
above do not show.

```{r}
#| label: iep02-table-models
m_quadratic_known <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k,
  data = known_gender
)
summary(reduced)
summary(m_quadratic_known)
```

Column (1) is the reduced model of Task 2 (`reduced`), column (2) the
complete model of Task 2 (`complete`), column (3) the interaction model of
Task 3 (`m_interaction`), and column (4) the quadratic model
(`m_quadratic_known`).

::: {.reg-table}
| | (1) | (2) | (3) | (4) |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Season | −0.815\*\*\* | −0.824\*\*\* | −0.799\*\*\* | −1.713\*\*\* |
| | (0.047) | (0.048) | (0.066) | (0.206) |
| Season squared | | | | 0.051\*\*\* |
| | | | | (0.011) |
| Amount requested (\$1,000s) | −0.0029\*\*\* | −0.0027\*\*\* | −0.0027\*\*\* | −0.0027\*\*\* |
| | (0.0006) | (0.0006) | (0.0006) | (0.0006) |
| All-women team | | 1.284\*\* | | |
| | | (0.481) | | |
| Mixed team | | 0.121 | | |
| | | (0.541) | | |
| Team with women (all-women or mixed) | | | 0.807 | |
| | | | (0.412) | |
| Season × team with women | | | −0.061 | |
| | | | (0.096) | |
| Intercept | 21.185\*\*\* | 20.839\*\*\* | 13.625\*\*\* | 24.168\*\*\* |
| | (0.484) | (0.506) | (0.335) | (0.822) |
| Observations | 1,434 | 1,434 | 1,434 | 1,434 |
| $R^2$ | 0.187 | 0.191 | 0.189 | 0.198 |
| Adjusted $R^2$ | 0.186 | 0.189 | 0.187 | 0.197 |
:::

Outcome: equity offered (%). Ordinary least squares. Standard errors in
parentheses. All four columns use the same 1,434 pitches with a known team
classification. The reference category is all-men teams. In column (3) season
is centred at its mean (about 8.8), so the intercept and the coefficient of
"Team with women" refer to the average season.
\* p < 0.05, \*\* p < 0.01, \*\*\* p < 0.001.

Read along the Season row. The coefficient is close to $-0.8$ in
columns (1) to (3). In column (4) it is $-1.713$, because with the quadratic term in
the model the season coefficient alone is not the trend. Read down a column
to see one model. Columns (2), (3), and (4) each add terms to column (1), so
a partial F-test can compare each of them with column (1). The bottom rows
show that the four models fit almost equally well: adjusted $R^2$ lies
between 0.186 and 0.197, a difference of about one percentage point of the
variation in the equity offered. Use this layout for regression results in
your thesis.

### Task 5: Read a regression table from a paper

The table below is invented. It has the layout of a table in a research
paper, the same layout as the table above. The outcome is
entrepreneurial intention on a scale from 1 to 7, measured in a survey of
265 students. Self-efficacy is a score from 1 to 7 for how confident a
student is that he or she can start a business. The table does not show the
intercept. Some journals do this.

::: {.reg-table}
| | (1) | (2) |
|:---|---:|---:|
| Age (years) | 0.02 | 0.01 |
| | (0.02) | (0.02) |
| Female (1 = yes) | −0.21\* | −0.15 |
| | (0.10) | (0.10) |
| Prior entrepreneurial experience (1 = yes) | | 0.42\*\* |
| | | (0.13) |
| Entrepreneurial self-efficacy (1--7) | | 0.38\*\*\* |
| | | (0.07) |
| Observations | 265 | 265 |
| $R^2$ | 0.03 | 0.19 |
| Adjusted $R^2$ | 0.02 | 0.18 |
:::

Outcome: entrepreneurial intention (scale from 1 to 7). Ordinary least
squares. Standard errors in parentheses.
\* p < 0.05, \*\* p < 0.01, \*\*\* p < 0.001.

1. What do the numbers in parentheses and the stars mean? Check the stars
   of the self-efficacy coefficient with its t statistic. The critical
   value is $t_{0.975,\,260}=1.969$.
2. The coefficient of Female changes from $-0.21$ with a star in column (1)
   to $-0.15$ without a star in column (2). Explain what happened with the
   ideas of Lecture 4, and say what the missing star does and does not
   mean.
3. $R^2$ rises from 0.03 to 0.19. What does that say, and which test would
   show whether the two added predictors are jointly significant?

Use (copy and paste) this structure:

```text
Numbers in parentheses:
Stars:
t statistic of self-efficacy, and check of its stars:
What happened to the Female coefficient:
What the missing star does and does not mean:
What the rise in R-squared says:
Test of the two added predictors:
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

1. The numbers in parentheses are standard errors. The stars show the
   p-value of the two-sided t-test of each coefficient against zero. For
   self-efficacy, $t_{obs}=0.38/0.07\approx5.4$. This is far beyond the
   critical value $t_{0.975,\,260}$ = `qt(0.975, 260)` = 1.969, and p is
   below 0.001, so three stars are correct.
2. Model (2) holds two more variables fixed than model (1). The Female
   coefficient now compares women and men with the same experience and
   self-efficacy. In column (1), at the same age, the difference between women
   and men was 0.21 points. Part of this difference went together with differences in experience and self-efficacy. The missing star says that the
   confidence interval around $-0.15$ includes zero. It does not show that
   the difference is zero.
3. The two added predictors explain a further 16 percentage points of
   the variation in intentions in this sample. A partial F-test of the two
   nested models would show whether the two added predictors are jointly
   significant. It compares model (1) with model (2) on the same 265 students. If
   you have the data, `anova()` of the two fitted models gives this test.
:::

### Task 6: A/B test, moderator and mediator (Lectures 5 and 6)

&#40;a) An invented A/B test. An online shop for refurbished phones shows 120
new visitors either its current product page (`new_page = 0`) or a new page
with customer videos (`new_page = 1`). Chance decides which page each
visitor sees, 60 visitors per page. The outcome is the value of the first
order in euros.

```{r}
#| label: iep02-ab-test
set.seed(21)
# random assignment: 60 zeros (old page) and 60 ones (new page)
new_page <- sample(rep(c(0, 1), each = 60))
# invented order values in euros, with a true effect of 3 euros
order_value <- round(40 + 3 * new_page + rnorm(120, mean = 0, sd = 8), 2)
ab_shop <- data.frame(new_page, order_value)
```

Regress `order_value` on the treatment dummy `new_page`. Test in five steps,
with the critical value approach at the 5% level, whether the new page
changes the mean order value. The critical value is
$t_{0.975,\,118}=1.980$.
Explain in one or two sentences why $\hat\beta_1$ estimates the average
treatment effect of the new page. Judge its size as a percent of the mean
order value with the old page. Use (copy and paste) this structure:

```text
R code:
Hypotheses:
Test statistic:
Critical value and rejection region:
Observed value:
Conclusion:
Why the coefficient estimates the average treatment effect:
Size, as a percent of the mean order value with the old page:
```

&#40;b) A meal-kit start-up gives a discount coupon at random to half of its
customers. Customers with the coupon order more meal kits. The coupon raises
orders more for students than for other customers. The coupon also brings
customers to the website more often, and more visits go with more orders.
Which variable is a moderator, and which is a mediator? How does each one
appear in a regression of orders on the coupon dummy? Use (copy and paste)
this structure:

```text
Moderator, and how it appears in the regression:
Mediator, and how it appears in the regression:
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

&#40;a)

```{r}
#| label: iep02-ab-fit
ab_fit <- lm(order_value ~ new_page, data = ab_shop)
summary(ab_fit)$coefficients
qt(0.975, df = 118)
```

The mean order value is 39.09 euros with the old page (the intercept)
and $39.09+3.41=42.50$ euros with the new page.

1. **Hypotheses.** $H_0:\beta_1=0$, the new page has no effect on the mean
   order value. $H_1:\beta_1\ne0$. The significance level is 5%.
2. **Test statistic.** $T=\hat\beta_1/\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_1)$, with
   $df=n-k-1=118$.
3. **Critical value and rejection region.** $t_{0.975,\,118}=1.980$, from
   `qt(0.975, df = 118)`. Reject $H_0$ if $|t_{obs}|\ge1.980$.
4. **Observed value.** $t_{obs}=3.409/1.341\approx2.54$.
5. **Conclusion.** $2.54\ge1.980$, so reject $H_0$ (p $\approx$ 0.012). At
   the 5% level, the new page raises the mean order value.

Chance decided who saw the new page. So the two groups are alike on average
in everything else, measured or not, and the only systematic difference is
the page. That is why $\hat\beta_1\approx3.41$ euros estimates the average
treatment effect of the new page. It is about 8.7% of the mean order value
with the old page.

&#40;b)

- Student status is the moderator: it changes the slope of the coupon.
  It enters as an interaction, `lm(orders ~ coupon * student)`, and the
  coefficient of `coupon:student` is the difference in the coupon effect
  between students and other customers.
- Website visits are the mediator: they lie on the path from the coupon to
  orders. Adding visits, `lm(orders ~ coupon + visits)`, shrinks the coupon
  coefficient to the direct part. For the total effect of the coupon, leave
  visits out of the model.
:::

### Task 7: Check the AI (Lectures 4 to 6)

An invented example. Lisa runs a café on campus. On 150 days she recorded
the daily sales in euros, the number of flyers that she handed out that day,
the temperature, and whether the day was in an exam week. The data are
observational: Lisa decided herself on which days she handed out how many
flyers. She fitted a multiple regression and gave its output to an AI
assistant:

```text
Outcome: daily sales (€), 150 days       Estimate  Std. Error
Flyers handed out (100s)                     18.0         5.0
Temperature (°C)                              6.5         1.2
Exam week (1 = yes)                         -85.0        22.0
Intercept                                   420.0        35.0
```

The reference category of the dummy is days outside exam weeks. The
critical value for a 95% confidence interval and a 5% test is
$t_{0.975,\,146}=1.976$.

She asked: "Should I hand out more flyers?" The AI answered:

> "Your model controls for the temperature and for exam weeks. So it shows
> the causal effect of flyers: every 100 extra flyers will raise your daily
> sales by €18. In exam weeks, your café sells on average €85 less per day
> than on an average day. The 95% confidence interval of the flyer
> coefficient does not include zero, so the coefficient is significantly
> different from zero at the 5% level."

1. The AI answer contains exactly two errors. Name each error and explain
   it in one sentence.
2. Rewrite the two wrong statements so that the output supports them, in
   one sentence each.

Printing 100 flyers costs €3, and Lisa hands them out herself. Of each euro
of sales, 50 cents are left as margin after the direct costs.

3. Calculate the 95% confidence interval of the flyer coefficient. Then
   calculate the extra daily margin that goes with 100 more flyers, at the
   lower and at the upper end of the interval.
4. Decide whether Lisa should hand out 100 more flyers per day on the basis
   of these numbers, and give your reason in one sentence. Then explain in
   one sentence one reason why her true gain could differ from these
   numbers.

Use (copy and paste) this structure:

```text
First error:
Second error:
Correct sentence about the flyer coefficient:
Correct sentence about the exam-week coefficient:
Interval, calculation:
Interval:
Extra margin at both ends:
Decision and reason:
Why her true gain could differ:
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

```{r}
#| label: iep02-ai-check
#| include: false
# Checks the numbers of Task 7.
qt(0.975, 150 - 3 - 1)
ci_flyers <- 18 + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, 146) * 5
ci_flyers
0.5 * ci_flyers   # extra margin per day at both ends
```

1. Filled-in structure:
   - First error: the controls hold fixed only the temperature and exam
     weeks, and Lisa chose the flyer days herself, so other things on those
     days, for example an event on campus, can raise sales as well and the
     coefficient is not a causal effect.
   - Second error: the exam-week coefficient compares exam-week days with
     the reference category, days outside exam weeks, and not with an
     average day.
2. Filled-in structure:
   - Correct sentence about the flyer coefficient: "On days with the same
     temperature and exam-week status, 100 more flyers go with on average
     €18 higher fitted daily sales."
   - Correct sentence about the exam-week coefficient: "Days in an exam
     week have on average €85 lower fitted daily sales than days outside
     exam weeks with the same number of flyers and the same temperature."
3. Filled-in structure:
   - Interval, calculation: $18.0\pm1.976\times5.0=18.0\pm9.88$
   - Interval: from €8.12 to €27.88 of daily sales per 100 flyers
   - Extra margin at both ends: at 50 cents per euro,
     $0.5\times\text{€}8.12=\text{€}4.06$ and
     $0.5\times\text{€}27.88=\text{€}13.94$ per day.
4. Filled-in structure:
   - Decision and reason: hand out the extra flyers on this evidence. Even
     at the lower end of the interval, the extra margin of €4.06 is above
     the €3 that 100 flyers cost.
   - Why her true gain could differ: the coefficient is an association in
     observational data, and if Lisa handed out more flyers on days that
     were busy anyway, the true effect of extra flyers can be smaller.

The third sentence of the AI answer is correct: the interval from €8.12 to
€27.88 does not include zero.
:::
:::

Tank file. Use season, the requested amount in \$1,000s, the presenting
team, and one extension that you can justify: an interaction of season with

team categories (`gender`).

Your answer must include:

2. the code that prepares the data, so that someone else can repeat it

## Check a model structure

This model structure covers points 4 to 9.

4. A good solution could fit

   ```r
   m <- lm(
     equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k,
     data = known_gender
   )
   ```

   or a model with a quadratic term for season and the group dummies. Keep
   `season_c` and `women` in the model next to their interaction (the
   hierarchy principle).
5. Name the reference category. Interpret slopes that combine several
   coefficients, or differences between fitted values.
6. Use `anova()` to compare the model with a nested reduced model.
7. Inspect the residuals, including `rstandard()` and Cook's distance.
8. Plot fitted values inside Seasons 1--16.
9. The conclusion must say that the team categories are broad, that only
   broadcast pitches are in the file, and that the results therefore do not
   show a causal effect of gender or season.

:::: {.utility-prompt}
<span class="label">Two sentences about your own venture</span>

Think of your own venture, or any business you know well. Describe in two

## See an example, then write your own

Take a student-run venture that sells meal-prep boxes on campus. "Outcome: weekly orders. Predictors: advertising spend and price, plus a dummy for exam weeks and its interaction with advertising spend, because I believe advertising works mainly when students are on campus. The first limit is omitted variables: the weather affects both how many flyers I hand out and how many people are on campus, and nothing in my data measures it."

## Extra practice for home {#i-ep02-home}

This task practises the ANOVA table of Lecture 5 at home with an invented
example.

### Task 8: A one-way ANOVA (Lecture 5)

An invented one-way ANOVA. The online shop for refurbished phones of Task 6
records the delivery time in hours of 20 orders for each of three couriers.

```{r}
#| label: iep02-anova
set.seed(7)
courier <- factor(rep(c("cycle", "post", "van"), each = 20))
delivery_hours <- round(c(rnorm(20, 20, 6), rnorm(20, 26, 6),
                          rnorm(20, 22, 6)), 1)
deliveries <- data.frame(courier, delivery_hours)
```

Fit the regression of `delivery_hours` on `courier` and make its ANOVA
table. Which dummies does this regression use? What do its two dummy
coefficients say? Test in five steps, with the critical value approach at
the 5% level, whether the mean delivery time is the same for the three
couriers. The critical value of this F-test is 3.16. Use (copy and paste)
this structure:

```text
R code:
Dummies in the regression:
Meaning of the two dummy coefficients:
Hypotheses:
Test statistic, with both degrees of freedom:
Critical value and rejection region:
Observed value:
Conclusion:
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

```{r}
#| label: iep02-courier-fit
courier_fit <- lm(delivery_hours ~ courier, data = deliveries)
coef(courier_fit)
anova(courier_fit)
mean(deliveries$delivery_hours)   # overall mean
qf(0.95, 2, 57)
```

The ANOVA table comes from the regression of `delivery_hours` on two
dummies, `post` and `van`, with `cycle` as the reference category. The
intercept 22.65 hours is the mean of the cycle courier. The post courier
takes on average 3.94 hours longer, and the van courier 0.02 hours less.

1. **Hypotheses.**
   $H_0:\mu_{\text{cycle}}=\mu_{\text{post}}=\mu_{\text{van}}$.
   $H_1$: at least one mean differs. The significance level is 5%.
2. **Test statistic.** $F$ = mean square of `courier` divided by the mean
   square of the residuals, with $G-1=2$ and $n-G=57$ degrees of freedom.
3. **Critical value and rejection region.** The critical value is 3.16,
   from `qf(0.95, 2, 57)`. Reject $H_0$ if $F_{obs}\ge3.16$.
4. **Observed value.** $F_{obs}=103.62/35.11\approx2.95$.
5. **Conclusion.** $2.95<3.16$ (p $\approx$ 0.060), so do not reject
   $H_0$. At the 5% level, the data do not show that the mean delivery time
   differs between the couriers. This does not prove that the means are
   equal.

The largest difference, 3.95 hours between the post and the van courier,
is about 16% of the overall mean of 23.96 hours.
:::
